1.pericope_label: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure... I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats David's adultery as the likely occasion, which would place the psalm in a chronological series with three others, and describes a man 'distressed both in mind and body, forsaken by his friends'. Ellicott refuses to infer anything from the arrows, since the figure serves for disease, famine and judgment alike, and retranslates both the second and the sixth verses.

Calvin rejects the notion that the title names a tune as 'unnatural, and without foundation', reading it as a memorial David made lest he 'too soon forget the chastisement'. Gill turns the sores figurative, making the wounds the psalmist's sins, for which 'there is no healing but in a wounded Saviour'.

Clarke demolishes the versions' titles — 'never was a title more misplaced or less expressive of the contents' — keeps the arrows physical, and insists the sores cannot be understood 'in any figurative or metaphorical way', while admitting the disease cannot be identified.

Henry reads sickness as a time to 'set our sins in order before us, for our humiliation', and makes the arrows 'the terrors of God' which 'are sure to stick where they hit'. Spurgeon petitions rather than describes: 'turn not the rod into a sword, smite not so as to kill.'

Augustine expounds the title's remembrance of the Sabbath as the groaning of a man out of rest — 'happy he who is wretched after this manner!' — and separates the psalm's two verbs, since some who are rebuked are never corrected.

debates.question: Can anything be made of the psalm's title?

positions.view: No. The versions offer four incompatible headings and none fits: 'there is no mention of the Sabbath in it; there is no thanksgiving in it, for it is deeply penitential.'
The whole psalm hangs on it. 'The Sabbath is rest. Doubtless he was in some disquietude, who with groaning was calling the Sabbath to remembrance.'
It means what it says: a memorial, made so that the chastisement should not be forgotten and so that others might learn from it.

debates.question: Are the wounds real sores or figures for sin?

positions.view: Real. 'I do not see that we can understand the word in any figurative or metaphorical way'; the following words 'denote suppuration', by smell and by discharge.
Figures for sin, which wounds and festers, and is healed only in a wounded Saviour.

outliers.view: The only voice to build an entire exposition on a heading another commentator in the same catena declares worthless.

themes: O Lord, rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.
For thine arrows stick fast in me, and thy hand presseth me sore.
There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin.
For mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me.
My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness.
I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long.

7.pericope_label: For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease... My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the loathsome disease 'inflamed or inflammation', notes that the ancient versions took the word from another root and rendered it 'mockings', retranslates the eighth verse as 'I am become deadly cold, and am quite worn out', and hears the psalmist's appeal as 'the clutch of a drowning man'. Delitzsch marks the change of tone as 'the calm of weariness, but also of the rescue which shows itself from afar'.

Gill carries both senses of the disputed word, and lists three reasons the friends might have withdrawn — infection, the stench, or a case thought desperate — concluding that the withdrawal 'seems to be voluntary, and to proceed from neglect and contempt'.

Clarke corrects the disease to 'a burning', reads the failing strength and dimmed eyes medically, and declines to name the illness though he says he could: 'I forbear, because in this I might attribute to one what would be more especially descriptive of another.' Wesley lays down the governing rule, that 'we should not forsake the literal sense of the words without necessity'.

Spurgeon reads the palpitation as caused by desertion rather than disease — 'the soul seeks sympathy in sorrow, and if it finds none, its sorrowful heart-throbs are incessant' — and finds the comfort in being read without words: 'none more lonely than the broken-hearted sinner, yet hath he the Lord for his companion.'

debates.question: What does the word for the loathsome disease mean?

positions.view: A burning or inflammation, from a root meaning to scorch — a feverish disease breaking out on the body.
Or, from another root meaning to be made light of, contempt: the ancient versions render 'mockings', and the sufferer is 'vile in his own eyes'.

debates.question: Why do the friends stand aloof?

positions.view: From fear of infection, the stench of the wounds, or a case judged desperate — not from law but 'from neglect and contempt'.
From a theological verdict: they took him for 'one smitten of God' and 'thinking me an accursed being, they avoided me'.

outliers.view: The only voice to say he could identify the disease and then deliberately refuse to, on the ground that symptoms common in one country may point to a different illness in another.

themes: For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh.
I am feeble and sore broken: I have roared by reason of the disquietness of my heart.
Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee.
My heart panteth, my strength faileth me: as for the light of mine eyes, it also is gone from me.
My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.

12.pericope_label: They also that seek after my life lay snares for me... For I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the conditional force running through the sixteenth verse — 'Lest they should rejoice over me: Lest, when my foot slipped, they should vaunt themselves' — renders the reproofs 'replies or justifications', and supplies the test of the closing confession: 'the sorrow is for the sin itself, not for its miserable results.'

Gill reads the silence as imitation, the psalmist playing the deaf man as Saul and as Christ did, and later as the fruit of hope; he takes 'ready to halt' as readiness rather than weakness, the sufferer 'born for trouble and adversity' and so unsurprised by it.

Clarke grounds the silence in guilt — 'I was conscious of my guilt, I could not vindicate myself' — hears a courtroom in the word for reproofs, and raises a manuscript question about the divine name that no other voice touches. Wesley grounds the same silence in submission to a deserved punishment.

Henry indicts the enemies on five counts, ending with the observation that such men 'hate prayer even in those that pray for them'. Spurgeon feels the exposure of a watched life — 'the merest trip of the foot sets all the dogs of hell barking' — and answers slander with patience.

debates.question: Why does the psalmist answer nothing?

positions.view: Guilt. He could not vindicate himself and was 'obliged in silence to bear their insults'.
Submission. The silence testifies 'his acceptation of the punishment which he had brought upon himself'.
Imitation and hope: he acted 'the part of a deaf man' as Christ did before his accusers, and was calm because he expected to be heard.

debates.question: What is it to be 'ready to halt'?

positions.view: Infirmity — one who limps and is about to fall, unable 'to take one right step in the way of righteousness, unless strengthened by thee'.
Preparedness — the sufferer was 'prepared for it', having considered that he was born for adversity, 'so that when it came upon him it was no strange thing to him'.

outliers.view: The only voice to raise a manuscript variant in the divine name here, and to explain it from the practice of substituting one name for the other in reading.

themes: They also that seek after my life lay snares for me: and they that seek my hurt speak mischievous things, and imagine deceits all the day long.
But I, as a deaf man, heard not; and I was as a dumb man that openeth not his mouth.
Thus I was as a man that heareth not, and in whose mouth are no reproofs.
For in thee, O Lord, do I hope: thou wilt hear, O Lord my God.
For I said, Hear me, lest otherwise they should rejoice over me: when my foot slippeth, they magnify themselves against me.
For I am ready to halt, and my sorrow is continually before me.
For I will declare mine iniquity; I will be sorry for my sin.

19.pericope_label: But mine enemies are lively, and they are strong... Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation

schools.summary: Ellicott suspects that 'lively' should read 'without cause', on grounds of parallelism and comparison with a companion psalm. Delitzsch traces the interpolation found in five ancient versions back to Isaiah, and insists the psalm never resolves: 'the fides supplex is not changed into fides triumphans.'

Gill defends the received text by narrowing the sense — the enemies are alive neither spiritually nor merely naturally, but 'in great prosperity and worldly happiness' — and notices that the petition asks God to 'continue not to forsake', desertion having already begun.

Clarke proposes the same emendation as Ellicott, 'a change made by the half of one letter', reports the strange interpolation about the rejected beloved and admits 'whence this reading came I cannot conjecture', and closes the psalm with a warning that righteousness 'may be lost by giving way to a moment's temptation'. Wesley reads the enemies simply as 'thriving and flourishing'.

Spurgeon reads the last two words as possession rather than petition — 'not my Saviour only, but my salvation' — and finds a use in the urgency itself, since affliction 'gives new life to our pleading'.

positions.view: Yes — a change of half a letter, restoring the parallelism: 'without cause my enemies have strengthened themselves; and they who wrongfully hate me are multiplied'.
No. The received text means the enemies are prosperous and flourishing, brisk with worldly happiness.

debates.question: Does the psalm end in triumph?

positions.view: No. 'No lighting up of the darkness of wrath takes place. The fides supplex is not changed into fides triumphans' — only the two closing words point beyond.
Yes. 'He who has the Lord on his side has salvation in present possession'; faith foresees the issue and begins already to give God the glory of it.

outliers.view: The only voice to identify the source of the interpolation carried by five ancient versions, answering the very question another commentator in the catena leaves open.

themes: But mine enemies are lively, and they are strong: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied.
They also that render evil for good are mine adversaries; because I follow the thing that good is.
Forsake me not, O Lord: O my God, be not far from me.
Make haste to help me, O Lord my salvation.
